title: Damping, forced oscillations and resonance; Newton's law of gravitation and field strength
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: C03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; O04-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C03-1#N.3, O04-uk1#N.3, C03-1#N.8a, O04-uk1#N.5, O04-uk1#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gravitational field strength
items.clue: Force per unit mass on a small test mass, in N kg⁻¹.

items.label: Uniform field
items.clue: Model used near the surface, where g barely changes.

items.label: Inverse-square law
items.clue: Pattern in which doubling r divides the pull by four.

items.label: Light damping
items.clue: Condition in which the amplitude falls by roughly the same fraction on every cycle.

questions.stem: Two objects exert gravitational forces of magnitude F on each other. The mass of each object is doubled, and the distance between their centres is tripled. What is the new magnitude of the gravitational force that each object exerts on the other?

A lightly damped mass–spring system is released with an amplitude of 60 mm. After one complete oscillation its amplitude is 45 mm. The amplitude falls by the same fraction in each oscillation. What is the amplitude after three complete oscillations?
questions.explanation: Each amplitude is 0.75 × the previous one: 60 × 0.75³ = 25 mm.

questions.stem: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?

options.text: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.

questions.stem: Damping reduces the amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator from 40 mm to 20 mm. What fraction of the original oscillation energy has been transferred to the surroundings?

options.text: None, because the period has not changed

questions.explanation: E ∝ A². Half the amplitude leaves 1/4 of the energy, so 3/4 has been transferred to the surroundings.

questions.stem: A car's wing mirror buzzes violently at one engine speed. A rubber damper is fitted to the mirror's mounting. What happens now as the engine passes that speed?

options.text: The violent buzzing moves to a much higher engine speed.
The mirror stops responding to the engine at all.
It still buzzes most near the same engine speed, but far less.
It now buzzes strongly at every engine speed.

questions.explanation: Damping removes energy every cycle. The resonance peak stays at about the same frequency but is much lower (and broader).
